subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING OWNERSHIP OF CANADIAN INDUSTRY

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING OWNERSHIP OF CANADIAN INDUSTRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. In view of the government's growing apprehension over foreign ownership of Canadian companies, as revealed by the return to the cabinet of the hon. member for Davenport, the setting up of still another committee and the promise of the Prime Minister on television last night in respect of yet another white paper, is it the intention of the government to reject any future guide lines issued from Washington to firms operating in Canada?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING OWNERSHIP OF CANADIAN INDUSTRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, firms operating in Canada operate under Canadian law and consistent with any Canadian guide lines which might exist.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING OWNERSHIP OF CANADIAN INDUSTRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister in very ringing terms suggested last night that foreign enterprise must be subject to Canadian law only and responsive to Canadian policy. I wonder whether the Prime Minister could not be a little firmer in his reply to the effect that they will not be subject to any future guide lines from Washington.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING OWNERSHIP OF CANADIAN INDUSTRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, how could you be firmer than say "under Canadian law only and consistent with Canadian policy"?

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING OWNERSHIP OF CANADIAN INDUSTRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I also wish to ask the Prime Minister a question with respect to the telecast he made to the Canadian people last night in which it appeared that the Prime Minister was trying to ride two horses moving in opposite directions.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING OWNERSHIP OF CANADIAN INDUSTRY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING OWNERSHIP OF CANADIAN INDUSTRY
speechtext: I want to ask the Prime Minister about the statement to the effect that the objective of the government is to have Canadians own and control much more of our industry, and that for this purpose the government is going to pursue a policy of marshalling a greater measure of Canadian investment in Canadian industry. I would ask the Prime Minister whether th:s statement is a pious hope, or whether the government intends this year to introduce a legislative program to give effect to this pronouncement.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING OWNERSHIP OF CANADIAN INDUSTRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I know my hon. friend will not misunderstand me when I say that no one in this house knows more than he about riding two horses going in no direction.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING OWNERSHIP OF CANADIAN INDUSTRY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING OWNERSHIP OF CANADIAN INDUSTRY
speechtext:
The additional policies and proposals of the government with a view to increasing Canadian ownership of Canadian resources will be made known to the house in due course, and I hope there will be further progress made in this regard before the end of this year.


Inquiries of the Ministry

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING OWNERSHIP OF CANADIAN INDUSTRY
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. May I ask the Prime Minister whether the legislative program which the government has in mind will have to await the report of the cabinet committee and the task force which has been set up, or has the government now a legislative program which it intends to present to the house this year?

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING OWNERSHIP OF CANADIAN INDUSTRY
speechtext: There are items in the program that have already been announced to the house that concern the subject raised by my hon. friend. I would hope that the task force in question will be able to produce a report and the government will be able to make that a government report in the form of a white paper in time to assist the government and the house in working out further steps in that direction.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING OWNERSHIP OF CANADIAN INDUSTRY
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I would ask the right hon. Prime Minister whether he would object to including in the various private bills regarding insurance companies and the like which are currently before the house a provision for Canadian ownership similar to that contained in the Bank Act.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING OWNERSHIP OF CANADIAN INDUSTRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this matter is already covered in the Insurance Act in so far as federally incorporated companies are concerned.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING OWNERSHIP OF CANADIAN INDUSTRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the right hon. Prime Minister arising from answers he gave earlier about foreign ownership, particularly of insurance companies, under federal charter. I ask the question because I was bewildered by the previous answer. Is the right hon. gentleman saying to the house that there is now legislation limiting the foreign ownership of insurance companies under federal charter?

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING OWNERSHIP OF CANADIAN INDUSTRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that is the information the insurance department gave me.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE

speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, February 1, consideration of the motion of Mr. Hellyer for the second reading of Bill No. C-243, to amend the National Defence Act and other acts in consequence thereof.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
Before the house rose last evening I had been outlining some of the reasons for my support of the policy for the unification of the armed forces advanced by the Minister of National Defence. I suggested, too, that since defence policy is only a continuation of foreign policy, one of the reasons for so much confusion in this debate was the fact that the two committees at work in this area, the committee on foreign affairs and the committee on defence, have been separated whereas in reality they should have been one.
When I broke off at six o'clock, we were discussing the testimony of the generals who had taken part in the second world war, as evidenced by the voluminous memoirs they have written. There is a whole series of books on this subject: "Struggle for Europe" by Chester Wilmot; the memories of Douglas MacArthur, the diaries of Lord Allenbrook, the memoirs of Eisenhower, Bradley, Wavell, Lord Tedder and many others who have felt the need to put their deepest thoughts on paper. One theme runs through all these books; the need for unification of command to end inter-force conflict.
The question which always faced these people was how best to get the army, the navy and the air force to work together effectively.

DEBATES	February 2, 1967
It has always seemed to me, having read most of these memoirs, that General Eisenhower was a good general, not so much by reason of any military ability he may have possessed but because he could get other generals to work together in a concerted way. Under the terms of this bill the armed forces of Canada are to be unified. The conception of a unified command is a logical one. Indeed, as appears from the article which was read into the record the other night by the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. McNulty), there is evidence of the beginning of this process in Canada under a former minister of defence, Mr. Brooke Claxton.
If we take this concept and apply it logically there is no reason to stop with the unification of command. It is sensible, logical and realistic to extend the process right down to the bottom as far as it can be applied effectively. There are a variety of tasks which are common to all the services. There is no need for three services to employ three people to carry out, separately, work which could be done better and more economically on the basis of unification. If a man is an administrator in one area it seems reasonable to assume that he can administer in another. There are great savings to be gained in personnel, in time and in money by embarking on such a program as is now proposed.
Then again, since all those who make up the armed forces are serving their country, there seems no real reason for retaining separate uniforms, a separate rank structure separate forces and all the rest of the conventional paraphernalia. This bill completely reorganizes the structure of the armed forces. It is designed to bring the armed forces into line with the conditions and needs of society today. It is unthinkable to me that we should organize our armed forces today in accordance with concepts which possibly were relevant in the days of the first world war.
The armed forces must represent to a large extent the organization of the society which brings them into being, which depends upon them for its safety and which uses them as its instrument in the conduct of foreign affairs.
This is a revolutionary measure. The bill before us brings the armed forces into the second half of the twentieth century, taking account of the weapon technology of 1967 and the 1970's. I believe it to be as revolutionary as some of the social service measures which have been brought down by this government during the past year. I think, for example, of the concept of the guaranteed annual income which will give us a new approach to social
February 2, 1967	COMMONS
security. So too I think this measure will revolutionize the organization of the armed forces.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
Some criticism has been advanced to the effect that we are the only ones engaged in this type of program. 1 ask the question, why should we follow? Why should we not lead? It is probably true that we are the only ones doing this, but on the other hand our needs are quite different to the needs of other countries. It behooves us to be responsible enough to provide ourselves with the tools to do the job we want to do. It is not necessary for us to follow the military structure of the super powers. It is necessary for us to create a force which will do what we want it to do.
In this debate a variety of surprising things have taken place. One is the charge that unification has been suddenly thrust upon an unsuspecting and unprepared parliament. I cannot understand this argument. If we go back to the time this government first was elected, we will recall that a special defence committee was set up. That committee looked into this matter. Then there was a white paper. Goodness knows the defence committee sat often enough. It had 81 meetings, 2,300 pages of evidence were recorded, and a total of 103 witnesses appeared. The associate minister was in attendance at 63 meetings, and the m nister answered some 857 questions. This does not take into account the amount of time we have dealt with defence matters in the House of Commons.
It seems to me that those who make such a charge are doing themselves a disservice, because it indicates that they did not do their homework, that they did not read the documents and were not prepared to debate the issue with regard to integration and unification.
Had these members done their homework and had they known what they were talking about, then during the committee meetings they would have taken the opportunity to probe the minister and his officials in order to get to the bottom of it. Instead, this only came out after a series of admirals had resigned from the service; that is, after there had been a so-called admirals' revolt. When this was going on I received a letter from one of my constituents who had served in the navy. He told me that if this was the most effective way the admirals could fight, he was very thankful they had left the service.

But in many cases their effectiveness in this area has not been what I would have liked it to be. However, I do withdraw the remarks. In any case, I hope we will soon have a vote on second reading so this bill can go to the committee to be properly investigated.
There has been a certain amount of energy directed toward the constitutional question which has amused me. It has been stated that the government should send the bill to the committee without having a vote on second reading on the principle of the matter. This seems to be completely at odds with the concept of responsible government. If the government is willing to accept the responsibility for bringing forth new legislation, and if the supporters of the government party are satisfied with it, then it seems to me the government is fulfilling its responsibility in bringing


National Defence Act Amendment a clear-cut program to the Canadian people. It appears to me that the only time the action of sending a matter to a committee for investigation would be warranted would be when the government had not made up its mind, when there was a great deal of dissention about the effectiveness of the matter, and when they were looking for additional information.
In the present circumstances, however, I think those who suggest that the measure should not be voted on before going to a committee are taking an irresponsible approach.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext: Is the hon. member suggesting that the Minister of Transport was irresponsible in sending the transportation bill to a committee of this house before the bill was given second reading?

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
As I understand it, the Minister of Transport referred Bill C-120 in 1964 to the committee for direction. As I said in my remarks, this should be done only when the government feels there is a great deal of dissention and where there is no firm opinion on the government side of the house concerning the effectiveness of the bill.
The other matter on which I should like to comment is the personal attack on the minister. It seems to me that this has displaced a good deal of good, honest debate which might have taken place. The minister may or may not have a propaganda machine backing him up, but this has nothing to do with the subject matter of the bill. One could be in favour of the bill without having to like the minister, and one could like the minister without having to like his bill. It seems to me, however, that we should be devoting our attention to the subject matter and the principle of this bill instead of using the bill as a cloak for a personal attack.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext: Or for attacking admirals.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
It seems to me that some of the behaviour we have seen in this house and some of the attacks which have been made by hon. members opposite tend to prove the old adage that people become more aroused over trivialities than they do over serious fundamentals, and that the amount of response often is in inverse ratio to the profundity of the issue.
I should like to close by quoting an anecdote about Albert Einstein. Mr. Einstein was once asked why it was that mankind, having


been clever enough to achieve the grand scale release of nuclear energy, was apparently unable to avert its use in the destruction of mankind. "That's very simple," Einstein replied. "It's because politics is far more complicated than physics." We certainly have seen an illustration of that in the debate on this bill.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to take part in a debate which is a bread and butter issue for my constituency as well as having the major ramifications of life and death.
First I must state my regret concerning the way in which the early part of this debate has progressed in this chamber. I think the minister brought no credit and probably demeaned himself by endorsing what really was a goon squad approach in allowing young and enthusiastic members of the Department of National Defence to engage in the debate while in the gallery of this house; not speaking out in the manner of rowdyism but exhibiting rowdyism none the less. If this is indicative of the mentality of the minister and those people, then I say they should all go; because past ministers of national defence and past military people in the Department of National Defence always were very careful to assert the civilian predominance over the military. This sort of approach, I presume derived from the truth squad of bygone days does not add to the minister's charm or reputation.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
I also regret that a publication entitled "An Address On Canadian Forces Reorganization", which purports to be a speech of the minister in the House of Commons, has been tampered with somewhat in its publication. It does not reflect the proceedings that took place in the House of Commons on that particular day. For example, all references to Mr. Speaker have been removed and there are other forms of editing such as cutting out the interjections of other members. In this sense I say there has been some tampering with the record and an attempt to present a picture to service people which is not really accurate. When page five is compared with Hansard it is apparent that some seven changes have been made. I do not think the minister or whoever was responsible for this has done himself any credit by such an abuse of the use of the record of parliament.
One point has been made over and over again and I merely mention it briefly. I refer


to the failure of the minister and the government to develop policy on an all-party basis. In other words, there has been no effort to develop a policy which would reflect the contributions of all members of parliament rather than the views of the minister. This is regrettable but the point has been made on several occasions and I do not intend to belabour it.
Our main concern relates to the objectives of military policy. The last speaker, drawing on the inexhaustible information he acquired in his political science course at university, pointed out that military policy is really an extension of the diplomatic policy of any country. That is true. Military policy may be either of an aggressive nature or a defensive nature. It can be fairly said of Canada that our policies have always been of a defensive nature and in line with our diplomatic objectives as a middle power trying to bring about an easing of tensions in the world.
The Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cadieux) in his thoughtful address yesterday, which I very much appreciated listening to and reading today, pointed out that military policy is an attempt to create a mix of peace-keeping functions in living up to our international obligations and our obligations in regard to the defence of Canada. These are worthy aims but the question arises whether the minister, the associate minister and the government are carrying on a course of action which will be the most effective in achieving these aims or are perhaps giving more attention to one part of the mix and not enough to another. My own view is that as a result of the bill now before us we are not going to achieve the utmost in value for our defence dollar and that what is being done will not be in the best interests of this country.
The question we must ask ourselves is whether unification will satisfy Canada's needs. Unity at the top seems to be acceptable, and unity in respect of supply and support services is probably acceptable. During an earlier debate I said that I had seen supply and support groups, engineers, ordnance men and the like working in a common service battalion at Camp Gagetown a couple of years ago. I was impressed by the operation and by the fact they seemed to be happy working together. Perhaps there can be no quarrel about the concept of unification in respect of supply and support services, though the minister and his department will find that because of the great degree of
1256S
National Defence Act Amendment specialization required in the different services this may be rather difficult to achieve.
The most resistance in respect of unification occurs at the combat level. Surely it is the combat level, which of all levels, must have efficiency, with which we must concern ourselves. We cannot blind ourselves to the opinions which have been expressed by those who might be termed traditionalists. A great friend of the minister-I assume they are still friends-has been quoted from time to time. I refer to R. S. Malone, publisher of the Winnipeg Free Press. Let me read something that has not yet been placed on the record so far as I am aware. Mr. Malone is quoted in the Bulletin of the maritime command, December 1966 issue, as follows:
In my view two cardinal errors have been made in our integration program. Before examining these in detail, however, let me say something on the subject of esprit de corps. For those who have ever been on active service no explanation is necessary. Every commander in history, however, is on record as to the all important value of regimental pride and spirit-from Caesar's legions to Napoleon's old guard-or in England-The Rifle Brigade, the "Buffs", the Grenadier Guards, the Scots Guards, the "Fore and Afts" and all the other units of fame and tradition... in Canada in the past hundred years we have built similar reputations for such regiments as the Black Watch, the Queen's Own, The Van Doos, the Patricias, the 48th, The Little Black Devils, The Seaforths, and so on, right across the country. All of these units, as well as our famous naval and air units, have come to mean something very real in our national structure. Thousands of men have given their lives in building these deserved reputations.
Comparing the respective values of esprit de corps to actual numbers in battle Napoleon placed the comparison in the ratio of 4 to 1.
That is the opinion of a person who certainly should not be classified as a "Colonel Blimp". If the minister thinks he is of that type he certainly has not publicly said so in respect of his dear old friend, Brigadier Malone.
The Naval Officers Associations of Canada, in dealing with the same subject in a letter of October 3 to the chairman of the standing committee on national defence, made this point at page five of their presentation:
-we have been conducting a survey since the spring of this year with the following results:
Only 25.3 per cent have been "combat" types, but 95.1 per cent of these men wanted to be quickly recognized as "air crew" or "sea going" or "land fighters". A distinctive cap and arm insignia did not appear to be considered as a distinctive uniform by naval and air force men. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the electors I represent here are concerned about this matter of unification and integration for various reasons. The first one is that we have at home a regiment which did our country proud during the last war and which, as a reserve regiment, is still very active. This matter is discussed on the principle that we believe in effectiveness, economy and competence in the organization of defence and all other government services.
I feel justified in saying to the house that all the people I represent approve of the unification and integration program for another reason, namely because General Allard, who is chief of staff of the armed forces, is one of our native sons. As a matter of fact, according to his biography, he was born in Sainte-Monique, in the riding of Nicolet, but he left when still quite young for Trois-Rivieres where he got his early schooling and experience. That is where he joined the army and his studies, hard work and competence earned him promotion after promotion. He enjoys the full confidence of our men.
When we heard that the government's unification and integration program had General Allard's full support, our people said: That's all right, we support it. And they asked me to express their views in the house.
What is it all about, Mr. Speaker? I said a word about it a while ago. The object is to make our defence system more efficient; it is to increase competence, to concentrate our technical skills, instead of leaving them


divided among three services; it is also to avoid disastrous delays which occur because of that multiplicity of commands and services; it is to avoid conflicts of authority which we so often witness in some countries, conflicts of prestige precisely because there is a great desire to uphold ancient traditions which very often result in ranks, dazzling uniforms or certain small prerogatives acquired through the centuries but do not meet modem army needs for efficiency.
Mr. Speaker, in order to define exactly what the object is, I have some literature which gives explanations that I should like to comment on, in order to circumscribe the debate. For instance, in reprinted articles in the Toronto Telegram, I find things that seem to be quite concise and quite to the point and which read as follows:

This requires unity of planning at all levels, especially in projects and priorities.
The other objective was most fire power, most flexibility and the fastest response possible for the taxpayers' dollar. The unified force would reduce duplication which has increased sharply over the years.
"Admirals and Air Marshals no longer have to write to each other when combined reserves are required," says Hellyer. "One unified command can work out a plan and issue orders, as combined operations did during the war.
This gives us instant decision making, which is more important than ever before."
In the process, there is more control over the military, as recommended by the Glassco commission's investigation of government operations.

And it goes on:

"Similarly, there is no lack of competition. The sailors will press for more ships, the soldiers for more tanks and the airmen for more planes.
This is as natural as breathing. Competition will not be lost, but it will be contained at the service level."

And a bit further, other advantages are listed:

A new single pay system is being developed in three stages over three years. By that time, when the system is fully automated, pay services will be provided with 650 fewer men.
Recruiting organization has been integrated. This has been discussed for 15 years, but there is no agreement among the services, which sometimes had their recruiting offices in the same building.
The new Canadian forces recruiting centres enlist officers and men for the army, navy and air force. Recruiting is higher than last year so far, but 23033-795J

National Defence Act Amendment
the job is being done with 30 per cent fewer people.
Before integration, there were five separate intelligence organizations at headquarters. Now, there is one.

And further on, we read:

Savings and an increase in efficiency are also expected from the new Canadian forces communications system.

So, that explains fully, for those of course who do not doubt the minister's word, what the aim is. It is crystal clear and should win over all those who really believe in the old proverb that unity is strength. Consequently, concentration of technical skills, especially in defence, more than anywhere else, will ensure the best results under the best circumstances.
Objections have been made, some of which are constructive and deserve to be brought forward in this house if we want to know the opinions held in all sectors of the Canadian people before passing the bill. On the other hand, some of them are whimisical and smack of some kind of personal aversion for the minister, and they result in criticism that, to my mind, should not be allowed in this house if I am to go by the rules founded on the century-old precepts of the gentlity which were explained to me upon my arrival here.
Other purely sentimental objections have been put forward; some people would like to maintain traditions charming in themselves, but certainly not fundamental qualifications for an adequate national defence system.
Concern over the possible disappearance of the pipers, or whether the kilts will be retained, lengthened or shortened, whether dress uniforms in each of the services will still be sine qua non, etc., in my opinion, this type of concern is imwarranted.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I think that if this were the hon. minister's only worry, he would readily tell everyone: "Keep your kilts and we will keep our pipers; if the French Canadians want their arrow sash, they can have it; but please, let us get on with unification and integration so that this first-rate defence force can be set up as quickly as possible, and in the best conditions."
Sentimental considerations do not agree very well with North American tradition; we were taught that two and two makes four


National Defence Act Amendment and that we should not let ourselves be influenced by traditions which are very nice in themselves, but surely not based on efficient administrative principles.
Mr. Speaker, some complain that the matter has not been adequately explained. I shall come back to this later. It seems to me that more than enough explanations have been given and that ample discussion has taken place. But at any rate, let us consider those criticisms as well-founded and suggest that the minister continue providing factual and specific explanations, so that no Canadian may complain of being kept in the dark concerning unification.
I say no Canadian of good will, because I notice some who refuse to understand, and there are none so blind as those who do not want to see, who do not really aim to provide an efficient and modem defence, but who pursue instead partisan concerns or personal grievances against the minister.
Some complain that we are proceeding too hastily. It might be, Mr. Speaker, that we are proceeding too quickly for some people. But in our day and age, if you are not quicker than your neighbour you may be too late very often. It is probably more so in the field of defence than anywhere else: The first one there will win the battle, not the last one. In the re-organization of our defence system, such a principle is surely useful and valuable.
I am somewhat surprised at the feud being carried out by the opposition-that is to say, I am surprised, yet I am not, because they obviously have a political opposition role to play and they intend to play it, except that expensive delays will occur as a result, for all concerned, But at least, they are fulfilling their role.
I cannot say as much for the admirals' revolt, Mr. Speaker, for I have always thought and many people share my views, that a reasonable defence system is required in this country. I believe in the military career and I have always felt that in their career, the military should have a basic principle that discipline is something fundamental and that the higher ranking the officer, the more he should set an example of discipline. Many of those admirals were more interested in playing politics than in setting an example for their subordinates. This may be one of the reasons for the weakening morale of our troops, if it has indeed weakened.
In my opinion, those who complain that these admirals had to resign their commission or were dismissed do not help the morale

of the armed forces nor that of the Canadian people, because it is true that the higher the rank of a soldier, the more he must set an example with regard to discipline, and it is not the admirals but the government in power which determines a national defence policy. Let the officers be consulted in time, I agree, but when consultations are over, it is time to submit. This has always been an unquestionable principle in any country which has tried to establish an efficient defence system. Therefore, I find the revolt of the admirals most objectionable.
Besides, there is an old American saying which is quite plain: Get in or get out. I think it applies to admirals and generals as far as government policies are concerned. Now, we have been talking about a unification policy for fifteen years, and I think it is time for action.
Some nostalgia will have to be overcome, of course. In all modern progress, old customs are discarded and many people sigh for the good old days. Every modern economic revolution is made in spite and at the expense of some of the keen feelings one might have had heretofore.
I have seen, for example, in a western paper I believe, an editorial entitled: "Are we losing our pride?" Then, to show that there should be national pride, the article spoke about flags, kilts, pipers, and that sort of things.
Mr. Speaker, if our national pride must be based on such artificial things, I believe that Canada's future is in danger. Our national pride should be based on a concern for efficiency at the lowest possible cost, on the belief that we have a defence system which is entirely adequate and which was able to derive maximum benefit from all the skills we attracted into it.
I have said, sir, that in my opinion, improper criticisms had been made in this debate. For the guidance of the house, I should like to note a number of them.
For instance, I did like the approach taken by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness)-perhaps I am mistaken as to the name of his riding-as well as that taken by the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Sherman), whose views I do not always share and who sometimes seems to be fanatic. But he gives facts, advances arguments, explains them his own way, although it may be in an intransigent way. But when I see certain other hon. members trying to tie the minister

to the stake, trying to attack his personality,
I am of the opinion that nothing is being settled. I should like to quote some cases in order to arrive at a conclusion which I believe the vast majority of my colleagues will approve.
The hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Nugent), referring to the minister, said, as reported on page 12477 of Hansard for January 31:
His prime purpose is to ensure his own greatness.
Mr. Speaker, if one started from that principle, one could say of the opposition members that their first objective is to further the political interests of the Conservative party. It would be just as unfair, Mr. Speaker; in fact, it would be mean. The hon. member went on:
This is the first time that parliament has ever been so affronted by any minister of the crown.
Parliament is affronted. I have heard many hon. members raise questions of privilege to protest against that affront to parliament.
The minister is guilty of tampering with evidence and he has done so for the purpose of ensuring that parliament does not get the information which is essential before it can decide-
Those are serious charges, Mr. Speaker, and I think that the hon. member who made them is serious. He added:
-it is sheer hypocrisy and I am amazed at the hon. member's effrontery in making such a suggestion to the house.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that the hon. member who made those serious charges should ask the house to have the minister called before the committee on privileges and elections if he really meant what he said. Then, after blaming the minister for not giving enough explanations, he said:

-we must even suspect his motives.

Mr. Speaker, to my mind those are unconsidered accusations. He continues by saying:
Certainly this is not the only insult which he has thrown at most of the top personnel-

But I feel, Mr. Speaker, that in this year of the centennial of confederation, our first concern should be to reinstate Canadian patriotism in the minds of all Canadians, reinstate the confidence Canadians have in their parliament. If, like the member for Edmonton-Strathcona and others, including the member for Cape Breton, whose riding I have forgotten, we take pleasure in discrediting one another, if like the members for Lapointe and Villeneuve (Messrs. Mr. Speaker, it seems to me we could discuss the pros and cons of unification and integration without attacking individuals and discrediting ourselves before public opinion. I cannot help but recall the old saying that those they would destroy, the gods make mad.
That may explain why, in too many spheres of Canadian life today, there is a lack of respect for parliament, but people are beginning to really think that parliament is made up of incompetents, individuals who are dishonest intellectually, if not morally, and who are pursuing greatly disquieting aims for the future of our country. I find such criticisms unseemly and improper in the House of Commons. I must point out, however, that a few of them were timely.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
For those of our colleagues who make such unseemly criticisms, who object to new methods in the defence reorganization, who attack any new policy proposed by a government which is keeping up with the times, I should like to recall that Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth, who will honour us with her visit this year, is much more broad-minded and noble-minded about the source of inspiration of government policies, about those responsible for them since they are in power and about those partly responsible, because they form the opposition.


National Defence Act Amendment
I shall simply quote two paragraphs from the speech made by Her Majesty on her last visit to Quebec city. She was then speaking about the future of Canada and the human race.
We must prepare for that future today among our fellow citizens, we must give explanations and express our views dispassionately while respecting the opinion of others-
Rather than disparaging each other, we should set the example of constructive discussion. This comment is mine. Now I quote:
The problems will founder in confusion if we do not learn to enlighten them with fraternity and humanity. Let the dialogue remain open and it will tend to unite men of good will. True patriotism does not preclude the understanding of the patriotism of others.
And she added:
The democratic system rests upon the conscious adhesion of the citizens. The role of the constitutional monarchy is to personify the democratic state, to sanction legitimate authority, to ensure the lawfulness of the methods, to guarantee the execution of the popular will.
In order that the inhabitants of a country may live happily, they must live in an atmosphere of confidence and affection. But a dynamic state must not fear to reconsider its political philosophy.
I repeat, and the Queen said it:
But a dynamic state must not fear to reconsider its political philosophy.
And to reconsider it in relation to present needs and modern progress.
So I say, Mr. Speaker, that the only practical discussion called for, in these circumstances, is the one carried on by some of our colleagues when, for instance, they tell the minister: We are not getting enough information. Some Canadian citizens are not getting sufficient information. Yet, information has been given, since the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. McNulty) said the other day as reported in Hansard on page 12476: Between October 31 and November 15, over 200,000 words covering nearly 250 pages were uttered during debate on the defence estimates, in committees. There were two committees on defence and they held 81 meetings, the proceedings of which cover 2,300 pages. Some 103 witnesses were called; the Minister of National Defence or the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cadieux) testified 63 times. There was opportunity to ask questions, since 857 have been recorded. Now then, if 857 questions were not enough to get an idea of what the minister had in mind in this regard, we should give up. I personally feel that these criticisms are uncalled for. At that time,


there were almost 250 pages of text containing 200,000 words. At that rate, one million words will probably be on the record. It might be a good idea to print some 20,000 copies of Hansard, or condense the debate, so that all Canadians may have the opportunity to see how extravagant some criticisms can be when they are not made in an objective manner, when one forgets the purpose of a bill. In this case, it is to ensure greater efficiency and modernization in the field of national defence, as in all other fields.
Mr. Speaker, it has also been argued that some servicemen objected to the plan. Of course, they have the right to do so. They have the right to object up to a certain point. But they no longer had this right, when it became a government order. Only one thing remained for them to do: to leave voluntarily or to be dismissed, as it happened.
The men and the soldiers who endorsed the principle of unification and integration have been listed. They are not just anybody or fools. I shall spare the house another such enumeration. Anyway, a rather complete list of names has been given by many hon. members who spoke before me. I shall mention only the case of General Allard, a French Canadian like me, for whom we have a great deal of respect. He did not usurp his post, but literally conquered it by his own strength. He is entirely in favour of unification and doing everything he can to implement the program, together with his many associates who have also endorsed the program.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, the views of these professional soldiers who acquired experience by visiting the defence arrangements of all the countries in the world and who rose to their rank through their knowledge and ability, should suffice to assure us that the minister is on the right track in speaking of integration and unification. Therefore, I should like to conclude by saying that there are 20 million Canadians who do not care whether we will have kilts or pipers tomorrow, or whether admirals will continue to parade in one uniform and generals in another, but who are interested in knowing whether the country can have the best equipment in the world, operated by the best technicians in the world and at the lowest possible price, so as to put as small a strain as possible on the taxpayers. That is what they are interested in.


The opposition has suggested that if most Canadians favoured unification, it was because the minister had made them believe that the moon was made of green cheese, had blinded them to the facts. I for one, Mr. Speaker, believe in the common sense of Canadians. I think, on the contrary, and the opposition has admitted it, that the great majority of the Canadian people supports the government on the question of unification and integration, and that should be sufficient reason for members of parliament not to go against public opinion so eloquently expressed.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, I will support as much as I can, the policy of the government regarding unification and integration.

-when I saw a man with such experience, holding an absolutely necessary position, realize the urgent need of the Canadian forces-

The second option available to us was to commit all our forces to the deterrence of war by making additional contributions to NATO and NORAD. The third was to maintain only such forces as would be required to uphold our national sovereignty. The associate minister told us that a fourth option had finally been chosen. I quote from page 12536:
This is the option we have taken. This is the option which permits us to create a proper mix of forces which can be used to contribute to international peace keeping, which can be used to maintain our national sovereignty.
I maintain, in reply to the minister's argument, that the type of force we now have is most suited for these purposes and that it has proven to be so. In the first place, it has proven itself to be satisfactory. We have played an important part in NATO and NORAD, and since the present set-up of our armed forces corresponds with that of our various allies I believe we are more likely to

continue to make an effective contribution to those alliances by maintaining the structure we have at present.
In my opinion it has also been shown that Canada has played a leading part in peace keeping. There has been no indication that the role which our forces have played in various parts of the world has been in any way unsatisfactory as a result of their conventional structure. Again, I think it has been amply demonstrated that the type of force now in being has proven to be adequate and satisfactory for our defence and for the protection of the security of Canada.
I submit that the priorities, objects and functions of the Canadian defence force should be in the following order. The first consideration should be the security and sovereignty of Canada. That is the number one priority by far. Number two priority should be participation in defence alliances and the third should be participation in United Nations peace-keeping tasks.
Although the government has not admitted this, it seems to me that according to their view of the matter the primary role of the unified defence service, if not immediately then in the future, is that of peace keeping for the United Nations. I am one who believes that if it is at all possible we should encourage the United Nations to set up a peacekeeping force on a regular basis. I think it would be contrary to the interest of Canada if we unilaterally set up such a force for that purpose. When the time comes for such an international United Nations peace keeping force to be established, the type of force which should be established must be determined by the United Nations, not by Canada. If we proceed now to set up a type of force with a peacekeeping function, in the future we might find that it would conflict with the decision made by the United Nations when such a police force is set up.

To me the attitude that we should create a single force with the major objective of performing a United Nations peace keeping function is part of the kind of continentalism which seems to be common to the Liberal party. Republicanism or continentalism seems to be in line with such an idea.

I should like to quote again from the speech of the Associate Minister of National Defence. The reason I quote him is that he is the only one who has presented arguments which call for us to reply. Integration-to-unification is a series of interlocking steps designed to provide Canada the best military course possible to meet our international obligations for a reasonable expenditure.
I think what the associate minister did not realize was that the minister finally let the cat out of the bag when he said:
-the best military course possible to meet our international obligations for a reasonable expenditure.

One general principle should be underlined again [DOT]-the combat units will retain their identity and their specialized functions and training.

Separate and distinct uniforms.
Well, surely if 100,000 new uniforms have to be bought it is going to be more expensive. There will be 100,000 new uniforms of a different colour and type. Surely there can be no appreciable saving there. The second advantage is:
Separate personnel policies and the duplication of manpower required to support these policies.
Third:
Duplication in areas of common training.
Then, fourth:
Duplication of the communications systems.

Mr. Speaker, Bill No. C-243, which will provide a unified defence force for Canada, is a legislation which, in my opinion, has the approval of the majority of Canadians.
Earlier this afternoon the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. McCleave) talked about the indifference of the people. I do not agree with him on that point, and I wonder whether the Canadian people are not rather indifferent to some passionate and emotional arguments put forward by the opposition.
For some, the people are unable to assess the results of such government action. But I wonder, Mr. Speaker, if actually the arguments put forward by those who object to the unification of our forces are really valid.


National Defence Act Amendment I agree with the hon. member who spoke before me, the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Chatterton) who said that those who are interested must voice their opinion during this debate; but I believe that some speeches should have followed a different course. The same member also referred to an editorial published in Victoria. I even blame editorials which inject matters of tradition, of royalty and republic into a debate such as this one which only seeks to improve our armed forces.
Mr. Speaker, all kinds of motives are ascribed to the hon. Minister of National Defence; he is accused of stubbornness, he is blamed for his determination and even his sense of responsibility is questioned. It is a pity, in my opinion, that in this house, in public, the sincerity and honesty of our public men can be questioned. Earlier, the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain) gave us a few examples of arguments which, in fact, were unwarranted and which do not improve the debate.
The present Minister of National Defence is just as sincere as his predecessors. He tries to assume his responsibilities in the best interest of everyone; he places before us a bill which is indeed right with our time, 1967, and consistent with our world commitments. I am even led to believe that the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) and the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) would probably have made the same decision if they were still minister of national defence.
Is it wrong to submit that ministerial decisions are always preceded by studies at the department level, by consultations with officials and the people responsible for their implementation? Of course, in the end, somebody has to make the decision. And I am sure that, even in this case, it was not made lightly and that everything was carefully thought out with a sole object in view: improving the efficiency of our armed forces and establishing a defence policy more suitable to our country and to our modern times.
It is nevertheless ridiculous to see the reaction of certain members in this house. They always blamed the present government for its lack of policy, for its rehashed policies, for following constantly the influence of our southern neighbours, for waiting too long before meeting problems, for its inability to take decisions. Now that we have before us

a legislation innovating in the field of defence, a first, a plan which many countries are considering, what happens? Everyone cries shame, is afraid of the venture, anticipates the worst, instead of encouraging and helping the minister to implement a legislative measure which will be to the credit of our country and will give a new dimension to our armed forces.
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, all those changes will not be made smoothly or without difficulties, since any change naturally brings about a little disruption, especially when men are concerned. This is quite normal. Are we afraid to meet the challenge?
Were the few retired officials who engaged in a pitched battle against unification also afraid to meet the challenge? I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that practically all members of the Canadian forces are able to meet such a challenge and to carry out this unification project, a "made in Canada" project.
Yet, in this debate an effort is made to have the minister contradict himself or others; an attempt is made to show that he has hidden the truth. We hear an exercise in semantics, quotations, so-called contradictions, and above all, efforts are being made so that the people will look upon the Minister of National Defence as a monster who wants to crush our poor little servicemen and get rid of those who will not submit to his requirements. How ridiculous. Those who are talking of arrogance should rather say of the minister: determination and conviction. Those accusing him of stubbornness should talk about decision and action. Those blaming him for his obstinacy should rather see a sense of responsibility.
Mr. Speaker, I too have been a member of the committee on national defence since 1963, as well as the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), the critic in military matters of the official opposition, and I do not contend that somebody tried to hide anything from me. I am convinced that we were given all the necessary opportunities during the 81 meetings to examine the defence policy of Canada, to hear statements from servicemen, former servicemen and civilians, to question them and also to read the special studies prepared for the committee.
The minister, or the associate minister (Mr. Cadieux), attended 63 meetings of the committee. They answered a considerable number of questions, namely over 800. If certain senior military officers who gave evidence before the committee on the Canadian defence policy feel

frustrated because their evidence was reviewed before they could present it, I am surprised at their attitude, all the more so because they were able, while answering questions from members of the committee, to go far beyond the information embodied in their brief or in their statement.

I believe I can understand French; on page 19 of the white paper, I read:
Following the most careful and thoughtful consideration, the government has decided that there is only one adequate solution. It is the INTEGRATION of the armed forces of Canada under a single Chief of Defence Staff and a single Defence Staff. This will be the FIRST step toward a single UNIFIED defence force for Canada. The government cannot, if it is in earnest about the discharge of its responsibilities, wait many more months to introduce a bill it considers both necessary and pressing, and all the more so after having given a standing or special committee of the house the opportunity to study the matter for months on end and even years.
Let no one tell me that it is normal for the dissatisfaction of a few retired soldiers to

feared that the morale of our troops will greatly suffer.
Mr. Speaker, during consideration of this bill, the present and the future must be taken into account much more than the past. Efficiency must take precedence over sentiment; nor should the returns we can obtain from our national defence dollar be overlooked.
Sentimental and fond of custom and tradition though we may be, we also must be progressive and face our problems. Everyone knows that in this house, no one dares change too rapidly the procedures and precedents going back a number of years, precisely to spare the feelings of some of us.
In the meantime, however, the population of Canada is paying the cost of long discussions.
Mr. Speaker, I have personally served in the Canadian air force during the war, I was proud of my squadron and of the Royal Canadian Air Force, or the Corps deviation royal canadien as it was then called in French, but I was particularly proud of being a Canadian and equally proud of the exploits of each of our three services, at sea as in the air or on the ground. I was even sorry that our navy was not identified by a more distinctive insignia to separate it more clearly from the royal navy.
After the war, I was active in reserve troops in an anti-aircraft regiment for about eight years. There, too, I am happy to say, I was proud of my regiment and I showed as much eagerness in my work as artillery officer as when I was officer in the air force. Today, I have a certain attachment to both, and I remain proud to be Canadian.
However, in the present case, there is no question of transferring sailors to the army, soldiers to the air force or airmen to the navy. The minister said it, General Allard said it and it was the talk of the town but some are still afraid. The point is simply to set up a single force composed of several elements, a unified force so that its efforts will be better co-ordinated under a single leadership, with much more flexibility in action.
I think that the emotional problem has to be put aside, at least for the time being. Besides, the emotion is felt a little more among former and present military people who have lived through the last war, than among our young people who now join our services, either for a few years or to make a career out of it. However, the latter group is still the larger, it is where the fighting force is.


Therefore, let us give those young people the opportunity to extend their affection to the whole Canadian forces, rather than to a single service and very soon, they will develop a feeling of pride and generosity even greater toward their country, all the more because they will know that many countries of the world are watching Canada and this unification project.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
As for the uniform, it is again a passionate matter. The minister said that the military heads will be responsible for it. Well, I am prepared to place my confidence in them and I am convinced that they will choose a style which will meet all the requirements and which will even be attractive.
As for efficiency, integration certainly brought about improvements, for instance, the setting up of a single command-I think that everyone agrees with me on that-and the creation of the Canadian Forces Council, followed by the reorganization of headquarters and the structure of commands such as the mobile force command, the maritime command, the air defence command, the military command, and the air transport and materiel command. Already, it is possible to show that great savings have been made with an increased efficiency and a reduced staff.
With unification, we shall complete the process so that our three present services may benefit from a better co-ordination of effort in the field of administration, personnel training and the discharge of military jobs. Those who during the last war served in the army and in the air force, know full well that, at certain times, such lack of co-operation and co-ordination between our two services, was responsible for the loss of lives of some of our airmen and soldiers.
Yesterday afternoon the Associate Minister of Defence pointed out some weaknesses in our present system, from the rivalry between the three services to the duplication of our military establishments, of different logistic systems, to various communications networks, from the duplication of materiel purchases to the duplication in the training of the forces in each of the services, let alone the uniforms, various regulations and so on. For a country such as ours, to define clearly our aims in matters of defence is a must. Moreover, our defence program should contain some priorities in order that the best
National Defence Act Amendment possible use may be made of our establishments, our equipment and our financial resources.
Through unification we shall be able, with up-to-date armament and equipment, to protect our territorial sovereignty. We shall also be in a position to help prevent major conflicts through our contribution to deterrence forces, as, for instance, NATO forces, and maintain world peace while participating in operations under the United Nations, and all this with minimum strength and maximum effectiveness, which, in itself, will result in financial savings.
While setting up a single force, we shall assist in the establishment of better co-ordination and greater flexibility and mobility within each component of our armed forces.
Since that personnel must be replaced periodically, since some rotation is even advisable, each of those elements will thus be better prepared to play various roles according to immediate needs.
Our soldiers will be more versatile, our sailors, our airmen, our soldiers will be better prepared to work together and perform tasks as different as those called for by NATO mobile force, the defence of Canada and the protection of our territory, world peacekeeping operations, NATO deterrent force, help to the civil government in an emergency. All that through a more diversified training and equipment chosen precisely for more diversified use. For that very reason, the Canadian armed forces will be in a better position to face all kinds of emergencies, they will be better suited to periodic rotation and the government will be able, if need be, to change its international commitments without having to change drastically our military structures.
No doubt you noticed, Mr. Speaker, that I have purposely avoided so far to quote the views of any expert or soldier, because I wanted to express my own views without, for all that, feeling the need to repeat the various quotations which in general have already been heard in this debate or the previous ones on defence.
My personal views are based nonetheless on a thorough study of the matter and were arrived at following the work I did when I took part in the business and meetings of the special committee and the standing committee on national defence.
Mr. Speaker, the western world is watching Canada, it is taking considerable interest in our unification program. Let us join hands


National Defence Act Amendment and make this undertaking a complete success. And, if we really want to help the minister and our military leaders, let us make constructive and practical suggestions, as he recently asked us to do, and I am sure that request still stands today.
At the same time, we will be achieving this result through common effort, and I am sure that we will be proud of our accomplishment in the not too distant future.

Mr. Speaker, I have no hesitation in participating in the debate on such an important bill which affects a good number of my constituents physically and materially and affects the traditional and historic role and interest of the Atlantic provinces in the defence and defence forces of Canada. I must say I listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of the preceding speaker, the hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry (Mr. La-niel). He managed to keep the debate on a logical and unemotional basis but, with respect, I think he glossed over some of the cracks in the cake with the frosting of a few words.
It has surprised me during the four days we have been considering this bill, and it has only been four days, to hear speakers opposite, perhaps hoping to be constructive, continually refer to a committee that has been meeting for two or three years and a white paper that was published in 1964. This bill, once passed, is going to change forever and a day the form and substance of our armed forces. The minister is maintaining his usual silence, which is certainly most constructive fos debate, but I would ask him to tell me where, other than on page 19 of the white paper, there is mention of the word "unification" or the expression "a unified force".
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
I will follow the precept of the hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry and will not become unnecessarily emotional in this debate. I have had no military experience to bring to this house in trying to define the minister's concepts or in pointing out constructively some of the pitfalls. However, one thing that does concern me, which has been mentioned by others in the house with military experience, is what the experts outside the house think of this measure.
The hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry in frosting the cake, and perhaps
[Mr. Laniel.l
gilding the lily, will have to admit that there is a very real and sincere division about this issue among people most knowledgeable outside the house. For all the talk both in the press and in the house

and the government cannot have it both ways-the most constructive step that the Minister of National Defence could take would be to refer this question to a committee. The minister knows that this is the reason we are objecting so strongly and fundamentally to his bill.
During the debate on this subject last November many hon. members did not come out flatly against integration or unification but wanted the bill referred to a committee. With regard to the debate on interim supply last November we in this house know, and certainly the public know, that it was almost exclusively directed to the question of Admiral Landymore's evidence before the defence committee and whether or not it was changed either before or after he gave his evidence. That was the primary theme of the supply debate.
The testimony of the minister and his officers before the committee has been somewhat muddied by what we have heard from Admiral Landymore, and some attempt was made to introduce that evidence in the house. No less a person than General Foulkes, who occupied the highest military position in this land, suggested, with respect, that the minister was not as direct and purposeful in his evidence before the committee as he should have been. For instance, in 1964 the minister suggested in evidence that only the command structure of the forces should be integrated.
No doubt the minister or his advisers can provide me with exact information but, having read the 30 pages which comprise the white paper of 1964, as far as I can see the only time among all the thousands of words contained therein that the word "unification" is referred to is the one occasion mentioned by the hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry with reference to a single unified defence force. Only once is a unified structure mentioned.
There has been constant reference to the 1964 white paper and to the committee hearings based in part upon the white paper, but all of this as well as the supply debate in November was before the present bill came before the house. Surely, Mr. Speaker, if members of parliament are to earn their keep at all they must, when a bill as fundamental as this comes before them, define and dissect


it if they are not granted their one acknowledged wish which would resolve all matters for the time being anyway, the referring of the bill to the committee.
This is a constructive step that the minister could take but unfortunately he has not taken too many constructive steps thus far in response to the wishes and recommendations of those of this side of the house. That, of course, is his privilege. But in a way he should be complimented for putting the issue before us because for the first time in Canada, certainly since the conscription crisis debate during the last war, through the minister's action we are now at last concentrating our efforts upon the subject of defence and trying to ascertain what is our defence policy. As I say, Mr. Speaker, for that the minister is to be complimented.
Having complimented the minister for focusing attention on what the defence policy of this small nation of 20 million people should be in relation to the Goliath to the south of us consisting of 200 million people, the question must be given real scrutiny. In a way, perhaps this whole debate is academic. We all know that the shield and umbrella of the United States protect us in a meaningful way, and we on this side have tried to elicit from the minister whether it is the ultimate intention of the government to let the shield and umbrella to the south protect our shores and air space. Hon. members opposite may scoff at this, but I will not repeat all the arguments about sovereignty. Suffice it to say that references to the white paper, to the committee proceedings, to the revised evidence which was given and to the debate on supply are merely a red herring.
This bill was given first reading on November 7, 1966. It may be prophetic that December 7 was a day of infamy some years ago, and I hope that this date is not going to be symbolic as far as the effects of this bill on the defence forces of this country are concerned.
I realize it is the minister's belief that the bill will place Canada in a better state of preparation for defence than we were before. But many people more knowledgeable than the minister, let alone this member, have said that the bill will not fulfil this purpose. Therefore, what more constructive step can the minister take than to refer the matter to the committee?
The minister has had a very favourable press on this bill, and I do not begrudge him
National Defence Act Amendment that; it is understandable. As I say, I compliment the minister for focusing attention on this issue. But the minister has disappointed me. He has come from the booming area of Toronto with new ideas and new concepts to revolutionize parliament. To a certain degree he has a keen mind in many areas.
Having said that I suggest, with respect, that he has not followed his own principles in the one area he knows best, the area of construction. This is my reason for injecting the word "construction" into this debate. When you are mixing concrete and erecting a building it is not quite the same as radically changing an established structure and hoping you come up with a better one.
Let us suppose, Mr. Speaker, that in the course of his duties outside the house in the construction field the minister was planning a large building. Let us say that some of the architects, design engineers, even foremen and electricians employed by the consulting firm to prepare plans and specifications for the new building resigned. Would any reliable or successful contractor say; in the words of one famous admiral "Damn the torpedoes; full speed ahead"? I suppose we still have some torpedoes left, but I use that expression in the allegorical sense. I suggest that the construction industry would ride that particular contractor out of town if under those circumstances he decided to build.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Let us say there have been resignations and protests and that, as any reliable, responsible and reasonable contractor would do, a meeting is held to air the views of different men. A good contractor looks at things carefully, and I make no apologies for using the analogy of a contractor in this debate.

I shall not review in detail the arguments repeated here for the last four days. The hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) last night tried to show the history and chronology of the concept of unification as propounded by other governments. One cannot stress the points he raised enough. The subject matter of this debate is unification, not integration. Unification concerns us, as do defence policy and the sovereignty of this country.
Do efficiency and economy mean anything in the context of this bill when one considers what has happened in the forces in the last year? These questions concern us. What do we find? There has been a sort of stop and go, pause, retreat, change, reverse and forward action on the part of the Department of National Defence which has disproved the validity of what the minister has tried to maintain. In the forces we see a patchwork quilt of reaction and reflex actions. In these instant decisions that we have heard of the prime ingredients in the kitchen have not necessarily turned out to be for the good of decision making. Certainly the incident of the 500 pilots who were prematurely retired-one leading authority said that this decision cost the *Canadian taxpayer over $125 million-was not a positive contribution or a peg on which the minister can hang his hat. There was the howler hat incident, and that does not make members on this side of the house or the people of Canada feel particularly relaxed.

Then there was the "instant mix" decision on pilot pay increases which for the first time involved discrimination between air crew. This has now been resolved in part as a result of the general increase and the recent study of the salary structure. So there was a positive contribution in the end but for many months the situation caused dissatisfaction and erosion of men and morale. Again, the re-engagement bonus, though perhaps fine in theory, was not working out until the pay increases were announced last October. These decisions, I suggest, were nothing more than desperate reflex actions by the department at a time when they did not really know where their plan was taking them.
Much has been said about the efficiency and economy which will result from unification. Let us consider the question of economy. The minister can boast about results in certain areas but the over-all price tag, according to my information, is higher than it ever was.
I do not intend to review the command structure proposals, because the hon. member
National Defence Act Amendment for Queens showed us that no other country has followed the proposal contained in the bill before us, certainly not Britain and the United States, two large countries with a long military history. There has never been any complaint about the integration of command at the top level or about integration at many levels. Our criticism is directed toward unification at the lower levels, especially at the combat level. There is no objection to transport, dental, medical services and so on, being supplied by a single corps. But there should never be unification at the lower levels where combat is involved.
These are my views after reading the reports and the evidence presented before the defence committee. I suggest that the level at which unification might be applied should never be below the regimental level in the army, on the ships and in the squadrons. No less a person than Mr. R. S. Malone, in the course of a series of articles which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press, has pointed out the danger of unification at combat level. I do not know whether he has yet been quoted on this aspect, but he writes that the minister is trying to swim against the current which is flowing in other countries of the world, especially the United States. Mr. Malone is speaking about the decision not to impose unification at combat level. He says:
The same situation exists in the United States where an increasing effort is now being made to create and expand on regimental identification. To quote the U.S. Secretary for the Air Force, "men have functioned most effectively as members of an identifiable group. The spirit of unity ... of brotherhood ... is enhanced by tradition, pride in one's organization and by a distinctive uniform which is a mark of membership.
The value of esprit de corps cannot be measured with precision.
This is very different from something like concrete which can be measured with precision. That is why progress toward a unified command is so different, in one sense, from the construction of a supermarket, for example. The writer continues:
No price tag can be placed on it. yet we all recognize its intrinsic contribution in the quality of our armed forces. It is the heart of the true fighting force.
We should not tamper with that precious esprit de corps, that sense of identification, by immersing it in a vast agglomeration of a single service."
I ask the hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry to consider carefully this expression of opinion by Mr. Malone, a man who, if he ran for political office, would certainly not sit on this side of the house. He is fairly well identified, I think, with one party, or at least

He said: Mr. Speaker, this is a bill to continue as a federal company a company which is an existing Ontario company, in fact, one of the leading insurance companies in Canada.
[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)
The Excelsior Life Insurance Company was incorporated under the laws of the province of Ontario by letters patent dated August 7, 1889. It has been licensed with the federal Department of Insurance since June 23, 1897.
[Mr. Nowlan.)
I understand that, in terms of assets and over $1 billion of insurance in force, it is one of the largest insurance companies in Canada. As a provincial company the Excelsior Life Insurance Company is subject to most of the provisions of the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act to which it would be subject as a federal company, but at the same time it is subject to the jurisdiction of the Ontario Corporations Act, certain provisions of which overlap and conflict with the provisions of the federal act. This dual jurisdiction does result in some hardship and inconvenience. The company, for instance, must prepare its annual statement in the form prescribed by the federal Department of Insurance, but its annual report is prepared on a different basis to comply with the provisions of the Ontario Corporations Act. The Ontario act, of course, is designed to apply to all Ontario corporations and not particularly to companies engaged in the insurance business.
The investment powers under the Corporations Act in Ontario do not conform to those provided for under the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act. The provisions of the federal act, however, are the standards referred to in the investment community.
The company is engaged in direct competition with federally incorporated companies and with British and foreign companies operating in Canada, and it feels prejudiced by the narrow investment powers which it has under the Corporations Act of Ontario.
In some respects the Ontario legislation is silent in respect of certain administrative procedures, and the company has been following, and must comply with, the more detailed federal requirements. There are certain areas of difference in the field of administration between the federal and provincial requirements. These could be resolved if the company became a federal company.
I understand that the Ontario Department of Insurance has been quite understanding in dealing with this company in its operations under these circumstances. The company, in fact, has been treated much as if it were a federal company. The Excelsior Life Insurance Company is licensed to operate in each province and to transact the business of life insurance, accident insurance and sickness insurance. The company carries on business in all the provinces of Canda.
Reincorporation as a federal company and subsequent sale and transfer of the company's assets to the new corporation is not in itself feasible in view of the size of the Excelsior


Life Insurance Company. First of all, there are close to 200,000 policyholders. There is more than $1 billion of insurance in force. It would be quite impracticable to transfer these policies to a federal company. Second, there are mortgage loans on real estate which are held by the company totalling approximately $68 million. It would not be feasible to register assignments of such a large number of mortgages to a new corporation. Third, the company has marketable securities to a value in excess of $83 million. The task of transferring these securities would be quite onerous.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to achieve the effect of reincorporation as a federal company without the apparent difficulties posed by that course of action. This bill, by a special act, would make The Excelsior Life Insurance Company, a company of long standing and high reputation throughout Canada, a federal company subject to all the controls and federal laws to which it is now subject and make it if anything more competitive with other companies in the field and enable it to serve the public interest better.

I should think they would be revealing as well to the government and would give the government, if it needs it and I hope it does not, an additional reason to spur on its consideration of the degree to which Canadian law should apply to companies of this sort or companies generally operating in the field of handling other people's money, which includes life insurance companies, other insurance companies, trust companies, loan companies, investment companies and the like.
